messages.author: 94866edf3707c5ee
messages.subject: Project proposal GSoC13/R: clean-room re-coding of the Akima interpolation algorithm(s)
parts:
Over the past few years, we've been trying to reduce the impact of non-free software licenses, but the CRAN akima package for interpolation is under:

http://www.acm.org/publications/policies/softwarecrnotice

which is "solely for academic, research and other similar noncommercial uses, subject to the following conditions ..."

This means that all CRAN packages that Depends: on it are limited in propagation. Soon, at the request of institutions using CRAN, including universities, we'll be providing a stronger filter allowing them to avoid potential creeping license risk by limiting downloads to free licenses with only free Depends:.

So we need a clean-room re-coding of Akima's algorithm for interpolation.

Could the administrators consider adding this to the table in the Wiki? Would a short description to link to the table help? Daniel McMillen (CRAN/McSpatial) has kindly agreed to co-mentor.

Roger Bivand

messages.author: 94866edf3707c5ee
messages.subject: Re: Project proposal GSoC13/R: clean-room re-coding of the Akima interpolation algorithm(s)
parts:
Thanks for your expression of interest. The test for prospective students will involve reviewing and analysing the use of the functions in the akima package in a sample of packages in CRAN, the comprehensive R archive network. Use of awk/sed on files in the man/ directories of the packages using akima may be a good way in - spotting and extracting uses of functions in akima; the source packages are all on CRAN in predictable locations for a given mirror.

I attach an RData file to load into R giving the names of packages that depend on, import or suggest akima. Reading the R admin. manual may show how the package system works; the pkgDepTools package from Bioconductor was used here to analyse the dependency tree of packages and generate the two character (string) vectors of names, which may not be unique.

Some uses are trivial, not altering the defaults used in the akima package, but others permit the user to modify arguments, and these will be the best test of a drop-in replacement. The test will be to set up an effective benchmark, so that we can know to what extent the drop-in replacement gives users the same or similar results, and the same or similar control over the results.

Of course, the examples in the help files in the akima package itself are a good place to start, but the other packages using akima may exercise it ways not anticipated by the package authors.

messages.author: b98e21751c27e8b9
messages.subject: Re: Project proposal GSoC13/R: clean-room re-coding of the Akima interpolation algorithm(s)
parts:
On 03/22/2013 09:55 AM, Brian Davidson wrote:
> I just want to make sure I get this clean room concept down, since I've
> heard it has made many difficulties for other groups (google vs oracle
> for instance).
>
> Of the Akima package that is used now, I am 100% positive I cannot use
> the code. My goal is going to be to replicate the API of the package. So
> should I use the man pages available for Akima in order to understand
> the output?

Correct.

I would probably focus on the GNU Scientific Library implementation of
the akima algorithm, since that's already in C, and sort out how to
write an R wrapper for it that would mirror the API of the existing R
akima function.

The manual is typically 'fair game' for clean room reimplementation.
Additionally, I'd probably look at the packages that depend or suggest
akima, and see if there are examples or tests that use it. These could
be tested against your new R wrappers.

Regards,

Brian
